lines.text: Your hands are mirror images. This year's Nobel Prize in Chemistry is about how one hand can take over.
lines.source_text: Your hands are mirror images. This year's Nobel Prize in Chemistry is about how one hand can take over.

lines.text: Many molecules come in two hands like that. Life is picky: your proteins use only one hand of each amino acid.
lines.source_text: Many molecules come in two hands like that. Life is picky: your proteins use only one hand of each amino acid.

lines.text: Yet a reaction left to itself makes both hands, fifty-fifty. A one-handed catalyst, a helper that isn't used up, can tip the balance.
lines.source_text: Yet a reaction left to itself makes both hands, fifty-fifty. A one-handed catalyst, a helper that isn't used up, can tip the balance.

lines.text: In nineteen fifty-three, Charles Frank wrote a recipe for one hand to take over completely. One: a one-handed catalyst; chemists had that by the early nineteen hundreds. Two: boost one hand and hold back the other. Three: a reaction that makes its own catalyst.
lines.source_text: In nineteen fifty-three, Charles Frank wrote a recipe for one hand to take over completely. One: a one-handed catalyst; chemists had that by the early nineteen hundreds. Two: boost one hand and hold back the other. Three: a reaction that makes its own catalyst.

lines.text: In nineteen eighty-six, Henri Kagan ticked box two. His insight: the catalyst's metal holds two pieces, so mixed hands make three kinds of pairs, and the mixed pair barely works. Start seventy-five to twenty-five, and the working catalysts are ninety to ten: a purer product than a straight line predicts.

lines.text: In nineteen ninety-five, Kenso Soai ticked box three: a molecule that helps build more of itself, same hand, from simple ingredients.
lines.source_text: In nineteen ninety-five, Kenso Soai ticked box three: a molecule that helps build more of itself, same hand, from simple ingredients.

lines.text: In two thousand three, his team started with a lead of five parts in ten million. Each run's product seeds the next: fifty-seven percent after one run, ninety-nine after two, past ninety-nine and a half after three.

lines.text: Then, with no one-handed ingredient added, the reaction still picked a hand, at random. In thirty-seven runs, nineteen leaned one way, eighteen the other.
lines.source_text: Then, with no one-handed ingredient added, the reaction still picked a hand, at random. In thirty-seven runs, nineteen leaned one way, eighteen the other.

lines.text: In our toy model, copying alone isn't enough: ten thousand runs end up anywhere. Add box two, where a one-hand and a mirror molecule pair up and stop working, and nearly every run ends with one hand taking over. Which hand is a coin toss.

lines.text: A toy, not how life chose its hand. The Nobel Committee stresses Frank's model isn't the answer to life's origin, and how Soai's reaction works is still debated.

lines.text: Choosing the hand matters for medicines: one form does the job, and its mirror image can cause unnecessary, sometimes harmful, side effects.
